chunks: How UART transmits and receives. The question: How does it work?
A UART has a sending half and a receiving half.
To send, it loads a byte into a shift register and pushes out a frame (the byte wrapped in a low start bit and a high stop bit) one bit at a time, each lasting one agreed bit time.
To receive, it watches for the falling edge (the drop from high to low) of a start bit.
Then it waits half a bit, and reads the line once per bit time, near the middle of each bit.
Imagine a starter's pistol and a flashing lamp. The pistol is the start bit. The lamp then shows one bit per beat, and you have a watch that counts beats.
You do not look at the lamp when it changes, because that is when it is blurry.
You wait half a beat after the pistol, then look at the middle of each beat, when the lamp is steadiest.
Software writes the byte (TXE drops), and TXE goes high again as soon as the byte moves into the shift register, long before the frame is finished.
The line is only done when the stop bit completes, which is what the separate transmission-complete (TC) flag reports.
Shift register: a row of storage cells that moves bits along one place per tick, turning a byte into a stream or back.
Baud-rate generator: a timer that divides the chip's clock down to the bit rate. Framing error: the stop bit was read low, which usually means the two speeds do not match.
Send the letter "H", stored as the byte 01001000, at 9600 baud. Each bit lasts about 104 microseconds.
The line goes low for the start bit, then sends the data bits rightmost first: 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0. Then it goes high for the stop bit.
The receiver sees the falling edge and waits 52 microseconds, half a bit. It confirms the line is still low, then reads once every 104 microseconds.
It collects the same eight bits and checks the stop bit. That is the whole idea.
"Transmit: the UART loads a byte into a shift register and sends a frame, a low start bit, the data bits LSB first, optional parity, then a high stop bit, each lasting one baud period.
Receive: it watches for the falling start edge, waits half a bit to confirm it and to centre itself, then samples every bit time in the middle of each bit and shifts the bits into a register.
It checks parity and that the stop bit is high, then flags the byte for the CPU. A bad stop bit means a framing error, usually a baud mismatch."
